title: Why Your Cron Job Runs at the Wrong Time (Even When the Expression Is Correct)
summary:
You write a cron expression, deploy your application, and expect a task to run at 9 AM.

But it runs at 6 PM.

The expression is valid. The scheduler is working.

So what went wrong?

Often, the problem isn't the cron syntax. It's the assumptions around it.

Here are three common scheduling mistakes.

  1. A cron expression doesn't specify a timezone

Consider this expression:

0 9 * * *

In a traditional five-field cron format, this means:

Run every day at 09:00.

But 09:00 in which timezone?

That depends on the environment and scheduler configuration.

If your server interprets the schedule in UTC, the task runs at 09:00 UTC.

For users in South Korea, that's 18:00 KST.

The cron expression itself isn't wrong. It just doesn't contain the timezone information you expected.

  1. Every 15 minutes doesn't mean 15 minutes after deployment

Consider:

*/15 * * * *

This means the job runs at minute 0, 15, 30, and 45 of each hour.

If you deploy at 10:07, it doesn't wait until 10:22.

The next scheduled execution is 10:15.

This difference matters when developers confuse fixed schedules with interval timers.

Cron describes matching clock times, not elapsed time since an application started.

  1. Daylight saving time can change the result

Imagine a daily task scheduled for 02:30 in a timezone that observes daylight saving time.

On the spring transition, that local time may not exist.

During the autumn transition, some local times occur twice.

Different schedulers handle these situations differently.

Depending on the implementation and configuration, a job can be skipped, repeated, or adjusted.

For time-sensitive operations, never assume that every local day contains exactly 24 hours.

How to avoid surprises

Before deploying a cron schedule:

Confirm whether your scheduler uses UTC, server-local time, or a configured timezone.

Check the next several execution times.

Verify whether your scheduler uses five-field or six-field expressions.

Document your intended timezone alongside the schedule.

Test daylight saving transitions if the job operates in affected regions.

For example, this JavaScript snippet shows how to display a UTC timestamp in Seoul time:

const date = new Date("2026-10-23T09:00:00Z");

const formatted = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", {
timeZone: "Asia/Seoul",
dateStyle: "medium",
timeStyle: "short"
}).format(date);

console.log(formatted);

It displays 18:00 in Seoul.

When debugging a scheduled task, always separate two questions:

What does the cron expression mean?

Which timezone does the scheduler use to interpret it?

Both need to be correct.

Preview your cron schedule

https://devrivettools.com/cron-generator

It's a convenient way to check expressions before using them in your application. Always verify the actual scheduler's timezone and cron dialect before deployment.

title: Auto‑Generate Docker‑Compose for Free‑Tier ML Experiments
summary:
Free‑tier cloud credits run out faster than expected – a single Jupyter notebook on a GPU spot instance can consume a 10 GB quota in under an hour. The bottleneck is not the model, it is the time spent wiring containers, mounting data, and reproducing the same environment on a new VM. ## 1. Define the experiment once, deploy everywhere
The most reliable way to keep the environment consistent across GCP Free Tier, Azure for Students, and AWS Free Tier is to describe it in a docker-compose.yml. Write the file once, then spin up a replica with a single command.

version: "3.9"
services:
 notebook:
 image: jupyter/datascience-notebook:latest
 ports:
 - "8888:8888"
 volumes:
 - ./work:/home/jovyan/work
 environment:
 - GRANT_SUDO=yes
 command: start-notebook.sh --NotebookApp.token=''
 tensorboard:
 image: tensorflow/tensorflow:2.13.0-jupyter
 ports:
 - "6006:6006"
 volumes:
 - ./logs:/logs
 command: tensorboard --logdir=/logs --host=0.0.0.0


python

Takeaway: Store the compose file in your repo; a single docker compose up -d reproduces the exact stack on any free‑tier VM. ## 2. Automate file generation with a Python helper
Manually editing YAML for each experiment is error‑prone. The snippet below generates a compose file based on a tiny JSON spec. It works on a laptop without extra dependencies.

import json, pathlib
spec = {
 "services": {
 "notebook": {
 "image": "jupyter/datascience-notebook:latest",
 "ports": ["8888:8888"],
 "volumes": ["./work:/home/jovyan/work"],
 "environment": ["GRANT_SUDO=yes"],
 "command": "start-notebook.sh --NotebookApp.token=''"
 },
 "tensorboard": {
 "image": "tensorflow/tensorflow:2.13.0-jupyter",
 "ports": ["6006:6006"],
 "volumes": ["./logs:/logs"],
 "command": "tensorboard --logdir=/logs --host=0.0.0.0"
 }
 }
}

out = pathlib.Path('docker-compose.yml')
out.write_text('version: "3.9"\nservices:\n')
for name, cfg in spec["services"].items():
 out.write_text(out.read_text() + f' {name}:\n')
 for k, v in cfg.items():
 if isinstance(v, list):
 out.write_text(out.read_text() + f' {k}:\n')
 for item in v:
 out.write_text(out.read_text() + f' - {item}\n')
 else:
 out.write_text(out.read_text() + f' {k}: {v}\n')
print('docker-compose.yml generated')

Run it with python gen_compose.py. The script can be extended to accept command‑line arguments for GPU count, Python version, or additional services. Takeaway: A few lines of Python replace repetitive YAML edits and keep the spec source‑controlled. ## 3. And deploy on three free‑tier providers without modification

GCP Free Tier (e2‑micro + Cloud Shell) 

# In Cloud Shell
git clone https://github.com/yourname/ml‑experiment.git && cd ml‑experiment
python gen_compose.py
docker compose up -d

The e2‑micro instance has only 0.6 vCPU, but the notebook runs fine for data‑preprocessing and small‑scale training. ### Azure for Students (B1S VM)

az vm create --resource-group ml-demo --name ml‑vm \
 --image UbuntuLTS --size B1s --generate-ssh-keys
az vm open-port --resource-group ml-demo --name ml‑vm --port 8888
ssh azureuser@
# inside VM
git clone https://github.com/yourname/ml‑experiment.git && cd ml‑experiment
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install docker-compose
python gen_compose.py
docker compose up -d

The B1S VM offers 1 vCPU and 1 GiB RAM, enough for a notebook that uses CPU‑only libraries. ### AWS Free Tier (t2.micro EC2)

aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0c02fb55956c7d316 \
 --instance-type t2.micro --key-name mykey --security-group-ids sg-12345 \
 --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=ml‑vm}]'
# Add inbound rules for 8888 and 6006 in the console
ssh -i mykey.pem ec2-user@
# inside EC2
sudo yum install -y docker
sudo systemctl start docker
sudo usermod -aG docker ec2-user
newgrp docker
git clone https://github.com/yourname/ml‑experiment.git && cd ml‑experiment
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install docker-compose
python gen_compose.py
docker compose up -d

All three clouds start the same containers, mount the same host directories, and expose identical ports. No provider‑specific Dockerfiles are needed. Takeaway: A single compose file and generator script let you move between free‑tier VMs with copy‑paste commands. ## 4. Keep data cheap and persistent across runs
Free tiers recycle the root volume after a stop/start cycle. Store experiment artefacts in a mounted bucket instead of the VM filesystem. * GCP: gcsfuse my-bucket ./work

  • Azure: blobfuse ./work --container-name=mycontainer --tmp-path=/mnt/blobfusetmp
  • AWS: s3fs my-bucket ./work -o iam_role=auto

Mount the bucket before docker compose up. The containers see the same path (./work) whether they run locally or on a cloud VM, and the data never counts against the VM quota. Takeaway: Bind a cloud storage fuse mount to the compose volume; you stay within free compute credits while keeping unlimited data. ## 5. Validate the environment automatically
A quick health check prevents wasted credits. Add a one‑off service that runs pip list inside the notebook container and exits with status 0 only if the expected packages are present.

 validator:
 image: jupyter/datascience-notebook:latest
 command: >
 bash -c "pip list | grep -E 'numpy|pandas|scikit-learn' && exit 0 || exit 1"
 depends_on:
 - notebook

Run docker compose up validator. If the command returns non‑zero, the CI pipeline (or a simple shell script) can abort the experiment before any GPU minutes are burned. Takeaway: A minimal validator service catches missing dependencies early, protecting scarce free credits. Act today: Clone the repo, run python gen_compose.py, then launch docker compose up -d on your local machine. The same commands will work unchanged on any free‑tier VM, giving you an instant, reproducible ML sandbox without spending a single credit.

title: Decarbonizing Peru’s Grid: Building an Interactive Wind & Solar Explorer for Paracas with Streamlit, Plotly, and GitHub Actions
summary:
💡 Executive Summary: Variable renewable energy assets face a fundamental challenge: weather-driven intermittency. In Peru's coastal desert, however, the intense thermal trade winds known as the Vientos Paracas surge during the very winter months when coastal fog attenuates solar irradiance. To investigate this natural synergy, we built an interactive analytics dashboard in pure Python using Streamlit and Plotly, backed by 5 years of daily satellite and reanalysis observations from NASA POWER (1,827 days), with automated CI/CD testing via GitHub Actions and continuous cloud deployment.

Project Links:

🚀 Live Cloud Dashboard · 📦 GitHub Repository · 🧪 Automated CI Pipeline · 🛰️ NASA POWER API

⚡ The Clean Energy Challenge in Coastal Peru

The transition toward a decarbonized electrical grid depends heavily on understanding meteorological dynamics. Traditional questions posed by energy engineers and grid planners are inherently multi-variable:

  • At what hub heights do coastal trade winds reach commercially viable velocities ($> 6.0\ m/s$)?
  • How severely does winter cloud cover degrade photovoltaic generation?
  • Can co-locating wind turbines and solar panels balance out generation profiles to deliver stable, base-load clean electricity?

In Peru, the coastal province of Paracas and Pisco (13.83°S, 76.25°W) is an exceptional natural laboratory. Situated along the Pacific Humboldt Current, the cold upwelling waters collide with the sun-scorched Atacama-Sechura coastal desert. This thermal gradient triggers the renowned Vientos Paracas—powerful southern trade winds that make this corridor home to Peru's flagship wind farms, including the Wayra Wind Project (132 MW).

Static PDF reports and spreadsheet exports cannot answer dynamic what-if engineering scenarios: What happens to capacity factor if cut-in speed is raised to 3.5 m/s? How many tons of $CO_2$ are displaced annually if we size a hybrid plant at 50 MW wind and 30 MW solar?

To answer these questions, we designed an interactive web dashboard that brings raw scientific data into an accessible, real-time exploratory interface.

🛠️ Selecting the Toolchain: The Case for Streamlit + Plotly

When developing data applications, visualization frameworks present distinct architectural tradeoffs:

Visualization Framework Primary Strength Architectural Consideration Fit for this Project
Seaborn / Matplotlib In-depth statistical plotting in Jupyter notebooks Static bitmaps, lacks interactive UI controls Ideal for initial EDA, not for production web dashboards
Bokeh Standalone HTML serialization with client-side JavaScript callbacks Extremely fast for simple 1-2 widget views; requires a dedicated Bokeh Server for complex reactive state Excellent for serverless single-page widgets; heavier to maintain for multi-tab apps
Dash (Plotly) Enterprise full-stack reactive applications Demands explicit Flask boilerplate, CSS layouts, and callback decorators Powerful, but slower iteration velocity for rapid prototyping
Streamlit Converts Python scripts into reactive web applications with zero HTML/JS Executes top-to-bottom; relies on @st.cache_data for high performance Chosen tool: Fast declarative UI, seamless Plotly integration, pure Python ecosystem

Combining Streamlit for application layout and Plotly for hardware-accelerated interactive visualizations allowed us to build an executive-grade analytics platform with sub-second filter response times.

🛰️ The Scientific Data Layer: NASA POWER (2020–2024)

Rather than simulating synthetic dummy variables, the dashboard is anchored by 5 complete years of real observations (1,827 daily records) retrieved from the NASA Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) project.

Target Node Specifications:

  • Location: Paracas / Pisco Clean Energy Corridor, Ica, Peru
  • Coordinates: Latitude -13.83° S, Longitude -76.25° W
  • Temporal Window: January 1, 2020 to December 31, 2024 (1,827 daily records)
  • Key Parameters:
    • T2M: Temperature at 2 meters (°C)
    • ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN: Daily solar irradiance ($kWh/m^2/day$)
    • WS50M: Wind speed at commercial hub height (50 meters, $m/s$)
    • WS10M: Wind speed at standard surface anemometer height (10 meters, $m/s$)
    • WD50M: Wind direction at 50 meters (degrees azimuth)
    • RH2M: Relative humidity (%)

Architectural Decision: Deterministic Data Snapshot

Instead of making synchronous HTTP requests to NASA's API on every user visit (which would risk rate limits, slow initial page loads, and third-party downtime), we wrote fetch_data.py to curate and bundle a validated data snapshot in data/paracas_renewable_daily.csv accompanied by data/metadata.json.

This guarantees deterministic, instant loading across local environments and cloud servers.

📊 Inside the Analytical Engine: 5 Core Modules

The dashboard is structured around five focused analytical perspectives:

1. Dual-Axis Temporal Cycles & Rolling Trends

Daily weather data exhibits high day-to-day variance. To highlight underlying climatological patterns, the application computes 14-day rolling averages for both wind velocity and solar irradiance. An interactive dual-axis Plotly line chart lets users track how seasonal fronts shift over the 5-year observation period.

2. 16-Sector Polar Wind Rose & Weibull Distribution

To evaluate wind turbine orientation (azimuth), we bin all 1,827 daily directional records into a 16-compass-point polar bar chart, categorized into four velocity classes:

# Binning directions into 16 compass sectors (22.5° each)
bins = np.arange(0, 360 + 22.5, 22.5)
labels = ["N", "NNE", "NE", "ENE", "E", "ESE", "SE", "SSE", "S", "SSW", "SW", "WSW", "W", "WNW", "NW", "NNW"]

df_rose["speed_class"] = pd.cut(
    df_rose["wind_speed_50m_ms"],
    bins=[0, 4, 7, 10, 25],
    labels=["< 4 m/s (Low)", "4 - 7 m/s (Moderate)", "7 - 10 m/s (High)", "> 10 m/s (Gale)"]
)
df_rose["dir_sector"] = pd.cut(df_rose["wind_direction_50m_deg"] % 360, bins=bins, labels=labels, include_lowest=True)

The data reveals a striking geographic signature: over 70% of wind energy in Paracas originates from the South to South-Southwest (180°–210°), providing a clear design orientation for wind farm developers.

Additionally, the dashboard fits an empirical Weibull probability density curve ($k \approx 2.2$, $c \approx 8.1\ m/s$), standard in wind resource assessment.

3. The Wind-Solar Complementarity Matrix

The central scientific takeaway is captured in the complementarity tab:

  • Summer (Dec–Mar): Solar irradiance reaches its zenith ($> 7.2\ kWh/m^2/day$), offsetting lighter morning wind periods.
  • Winter & Spring (Jun–Nov): Dense coastal thermal gradients generate sustained afternoon and evening trade winds ($> 7.8\ m/s$), compensating for the seasonal dip in solar yields.

4. Interactive Hybrid Plant Yield Simulator

Users can configure custom asset capacities:

  • Wind Farm Capacity (MW): Uses a piecewise power curve model (cut-in $3.0\ m/s$, rated $12.0\ m/s$, cut-out $25.0\ m/s$).
  • Solar PV Capacity (MWp): Applies a system performance ratio ($PR = 0.78$) against incident daily irradiance.

The simulator outputs annual clean energy generation (MWh), equivalent Peruvian households electrified, and avoided metric tons of $CO_2$ relative to the Peruvian national grid (SEIN) thermal emission factor ($\approx 0.42\ tCO_2/MWh$).

5. Geospatial Context & Data Export

An embedded map displays the study coordinates alongside operating renewable facilities in the region (such as the Wayra Wind Farm in Marcona). A complete filtered CSV can be downloaded in memory with one click.

🏗️ GitOps Architecture: From Code to Global Deployment

The system follows modern continuous integration and delivery practices:

    end

    end

🧪 Automated Testing with GitHub Actions

To guarantee that code changes do not break production, we established an automated CI workflow in .github/workflows/ci.yml.

Every commit and pull request must clear three distinct quality gates:

  1. Static Analysis (Flake8): Checks for syntax errors, undefined names, and structural code violations: 
   flake8 . --count --select=E9,F63,F7,F82 --show-source --statistics
  1. Dataset Integrity Verification: Asserts that the pinned CSV snapshot contains at least 1,800 records and verifies that all expected meteorological columns exist.
  2. Headless Startup Smoke Test: Boots Streamlit in headless mode for 12 seconds to ensure all UI widgets compile without throwing unhandled exceptions: 
   timeout 12s streamlit run app.py --server.headless=true --server.port=8501 || [ $? -eq 124 ]

With this automated test suite, regressions are caught before they ever reach end users.

☁️ Zero-Downtime Deployment to Streamlit Community Cloud

The public application is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, connected directly to our GitHub repository:

  1. The repository is configured as public: GianfrancoArocutipa/paracas-renewable-energy-explorer.
  2. Within the Streamlit Cloud console, we link the repository, set the branch to main, and designate app.py as the entrypoint.
  3. Every subsequent git push to main triggers a zero-downtime rolling reload in the cloud container.

In Peru's coastal desert, however, the intense thermal trade winds known as the Vientos Paracas surge during the very winter months when coastal fog attenuates solar irradiance. To investigate this natural synergy, we built an interactive analytics dashboard in pure Python using Streamlit and Plotly, backed by 5 years of daily satellite and reanalysis observations from NASA POWER (1,827 days), with automated CI/CD testing via GitHub Actions and continuous cloud deployment.

Project Links:

🚀 Live Cloud Dashboard · 📦 GitHub Repository · 🧪 Automated CI Pipeline · 🛰️ NASA POWER API

⚡ The Clean Energy Challenge in Coastal Peru

The transition toward a decarbonized electrical grid depends heavily on understanding meteorological dynamics. Traditional questions posed by energy engineers and grid planners are inherently multi-variable:

  • At what hub heights do coastal trade winds reach commercially viable velocities ($> 6.0\ m/s$)?
  • How severely does winter cloud cover degrade photovoltaic generation?
  • Can co-locating wind turbines and solar panels balance out generation profiles to deliver stable, base-load clean electricity?

In Peru, the coastal province of Paracas and Pisco (13.83°S, 76.25°W) is an exceptional natural laboratory. Situated along the Pacific Humboldt Current, the cold upwelling waters collide with the sun-scorched Atacama-Sechura coastal desert. This thermal gradient triggers the renowned Vientos Paracas—powerful southern trade winds that make this corridor home to Peru's flagship wind farms, including the Wayra Wind Project (132 MW).

Static PDF reports and spreadsheet exports cannot answer dynamic what-if engineering scenarios: What happens to capacity factor if cut-in speed is raised to 3.5 m/s? How many tons of $CO_2$ are displaced annually if we size a hybrid plant at 50 MW wind and 30 MW solar?

To answer these questions, we designed an interactive web dashboard that brings raw scientific data into an accessible, real-time exploratory interface.

🛠️ Selecting the Toolchain: The Case for Streamlit + Plotly

Bokeh Standalone HTML serialization with client-side JavaScript callbacks Extremely fast for simple 1-2 widget views; requires a dedicated Bokeh Server for complex reactive state Excellent for serverless single-page widgets; heavier to maintain for multi-tab apps
Dash (Plotly) Enterprise full-stack reactive applications Demands explicit Flask boilerplate, CSS layouts, and callback decorators Powerful, but slower iteration velocity for rapid prototyping

🛰️ The Scientific Data Layer: NASA POWER (2020–2024)

  • Location: Paracas / Pisco Clean Energy Corridor, Ica, Peru
  • Coordinates: Latitude -13.83° S, Longitude -76.25° W
  • Temporal Window: January 1, 2020 to December 31, 2024 (1,827 daily records)
  • Key Parameters:
    • T2M: Temperature at 2 meters (°C)
    • ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN: Daily solar irradiance ($kWh/m^2/day$)
    • WS50M: Wind speed at commercial hub height (50 meters, $m/s$)
    • WS10M: Wind speed at standard surface anemometer height (10 meters, $m/s$)
    • WD50M: Wind direction at 50 meters (degrees azimuth)
    • RH2M: Relative humidity (%)

Instead of making synchronous HTTP requests to NASA's API on every user visit (which would risk rate limits, slow initial page loads, and third-party downtime), we wrote fetch_data.py to curate and bundle a validated data snapshot in data/paracas_renewable_daily.csv accompanied by data/metadata.json.

📊 Inside the Analytical Engine: 5 Core Modules

The dashboard is structured around five focused analytical perspectives:

1. Dual-Axis Temporal Cycles & Rolling Trends

Daily weather data exhibits high day-to-day variance. To highlight underlying climatological patterns, the application computes 14-day rolling averages for both wind velocity and solar irradiance. An interactive dual-axis Plotly line chart lets users track how seasonal fronts shift over the 5-year observation period.

2. 16-Sector Polar Wind Rose & Weibull Distribution

To evaluate wind turbine orientation (azimuth), we bin all 1,827 daily directional records into a 16-compass-point polar bar chart, categorized into four velocity classes:

# Binning directions into 16 compass sectors (22.5° each)

labels = ["N", "NNE", "NE", "ENE", "E", "ESE", "SE", "SSE", "S", "SSW", "SW", "WSW", "W", "WNW", "NW", "NNW"]

df_rose["speed_class"] = pd.cut(
    df_rose["wind_speed_50m_ms"],
    bins=[0, 4, 7, 10, 25],
    labels=["< 4 m/s (Low)", "4 - 7 m/s (Moderate)", "7 - 10 m/s (High)", "> 10 m/s (Gale)"]
)
df_rose["dir_sector"] = pd.cut(df_rose["wind_direction_50m_deg"] % 360, bins=bins, labels=labels, include_lowest=True)

The data reveals a striking geographic signature: over 70% of wind energy in Paracas originates from the South to South-Southwest (180°–210°), providing a clear design orientation for wind farm developers.

Additionally, the dashboard fits an empirical Weibull probability density curve ($k \approx 2.2$, $c \approx 8.1\ m/s$), standard in wind resource assessment.

3. The Wind-Solar Complementarity Matrix

The central scientific takeaway is captured in the complementarity tab:

  • Summer (Dec–Mar): Solar irradiance reaches its zenith ($> 7.2\ kWh/m^2/day$), offsetting lighter morning wind periods.
  • Winter & Spring (Jun–Nov): Dense coastal thermal gradients generate sustained afternoon and evening trade winds ($> 7.8\ m/s$), compensating for the seasonal dip in solar yields.

title: Your AI Agents Are Logging In With Your Password. Banks Have Noticed.
summary:
Stop sharing your credentials with agents — per-agent identity is here, and here's the order to fix things in.

Disclosure: some links in the original are affiliate links, and we may earn a commission if you buy through them — at no extra cost to you. It doesn't change our analysis, and the security advice below is the same advice we'd give with no links at all.

You gave an agent a job. To do it, the agent needed to log in somewhere — a dashboard, a cloud console, a bank, a SaaS tool. So you did what almost every developer has done this year: you handed it your password, or a key that works just like one. It is probably still sitting in a prompt, a script, or a .env file you meant to clean up later. That is the quiet security debt of the agent era. Your agents are logging in as you, everywhere — and the institutions on the other end have started to notice.

How we put this together

We based this piece on vendor launch materials from 1Password and IDENTOS, reporting by Axios on bank responses to agentic activity, and 1Password's Developer Pulse survey of developers. Where a claim comes from a vendor — launch features, plan inclusion, partner lists, survey results — we label it as a vendor claim or cite the source by name. We have not hands-on tested 1Password for Agents or IDENTOS PolicyArc; this is researched analysis, not a product review.

Verdict

Stop sharing your own credentials with agents, starting now. Give each agent its own identity, scoped to one task, for a limited time, with a log you can read and a revoke button that works. Per-agent identity is becoming the default — 1Password for Agents and IDENTOS PolicyArc, both launched this week, are early, concrete versions of it. Fix in this order: inventory what your agents can reach, kill shared passwords, then add scoping, expiry, and audit.

Why banks are suddenly interested in your agents

Start with the bank's point of view, because it explains everything else.

According to Axios reporting, US banks are detecting unverified agentic activity on customer accounts. Chase has warned customers not to share their credentials with third-party agents. Read that warning carefully. The bank is not making a philosophical point about AI. It is telling you that when an automated agent signs in with your username and password, the bank cannot verify who — or what — is actually on the other end.

Mechanically, the bank is right. A legitimate agent using your password and a criminal using your stolen password produce nearly identical signals: correct credentials, an unfamiliar device or location, odd hours, rapid navigation, no human typing pattern. Fraud systems were built to flag exactly that shape of activity. Your agent does not look like innovation to a risk engine. It looks like account takeover that happens to be polite about it.

That distinction matters for you even if you never automate a bank login. The same pattern is now playing out across cloud consoles, payment dashboards, ad accounts, and production SaaS tools. When something goes wrong — a bad transaction, a deleted resource, a leaked export — the audit log will say you did it. Because as far as the system is concerned, you did. You gave the agent your identity, so every action it takes inherits your name, your permissions, and your liability.

And developers are doing this at scale, under real pressure to keep doing it. In 1Password's Developer Pulse survey, 65% of developers said they are expected or encouraged to use AI agents. Only 33% said they have a secure way to let agents sign in. That gap — between "you must use agents" and "here is a safe way to give them access" — is where passwords end up in prompts. It is not carelessness, mostly. It is a missing piece of infrastructure. This week, two companies shipped attempts to fill it.

The five ways agents sign in today, compared

There are really only five patterns in use right now. They are not equally good, and we are not going to pretend they are. Here they are, worst to best, with the two launches from this week placed where they belong.

1. Your shared password — the worst option, and still the most common

How it works: You give the agent your actual username and password. It stores them in a prompt, a script, a config file, or its own memory, and signs in exactly as you would.

Strength: It works with everything, immediately, with zero setup. That is the entire list of strengths.

Weakness: Everything else. The credential has your full permissions — no scoping, no expiry, no way to tell agent actions from your actions in a log. If the prompt leaks, the password leaks. If the agent is compromised, you are compromised. Rotating the password breaks every agent using it, so nobody rotates it. If you are doing this today, you are not alone — but you should treat it as an incident waiting for a date, not a workflow.

2. Long-lived API keys — better than a password, worse than you think

How it works: Instead of your password, the agent carries an API key — often created under your account, often with broad permissions, often valid until someone remembers to delete it.

Strength: At least it is separate from your human login, and most platforms let you revoke a key without changing your password. For machine-to-machine calls to a single API, this is a reasonable baseline.

Weakness: "Long-lived" is the problem. Keys get copied into repos, CI logs, screenshots, and chat transcripts. They rarely expire, rarely get scoped tightly, and rarely have a human in the loop when they are used. A leaked long-lived key with broad scope is a password with better branding.

3. Scoped, short-lived tokens — the right shape

How it works: The agent gets an OAuth-style token limited to specific permissions, for a specific service, for a short window — minutes or hours, not months. When the window closes, the token dies and a new one must be issued.

Strength: This is the pattern security teams actually want. Least privilege by default, automatic expiry, and a much smaller blast radius if a token leaks. A stolen token that expires in an hour and can only read one project is a bad day. A stolen password is a bad quarter.

Weakness: Support is uneven. Plenty of tools your agents need still do not offer fine-grained, short-lived tokens, and wiring up issuance and refresh for every agent and every service is real engineering work. The pattern is right; the ecosystem is still catching up.

4. Per-agent keys with human approval — 1Password for Agents

How it works: Each agent gets its own identity instead of borrowing yours. 1Password for Agents, launched October 22, 2026, is the clearest consumer-and-developer example so far. As 1Password describes it — a vendor claim, based on its launch materials — each AI agent signs in with its own unique digital key, you approve every sign-in attempt on your own device, and the actual password never reaches the agent. 1Password lists the feature as included in its Individual and Family plans via 1Password.com.

1Password names its launch partners as rolling out, including Meta's Muse and Grok Bot, with Claude Duet, ChatGPT Work/dots, and Townie listed as coming soon. It also says integrations are being built by Browserbase, Browser Use, Perplexity, and Ramp. Treat that partner list as a vendor roadmap claim until each integration is live and documented — but note the shape of it: browser agents and finance tooling are exactly where credential-sharing risk is highest.

Strength: The password never reaches the agent, every sign-in needs your approval on your device, and each agent is distinguishable from you and from every other agent. Revoking one agent does not mean changing your password everywhere.

Weakness: Human approval does not scale forever. Approving every sign-in works for high-value logins; it will chafe for agents that authenticate constantly in the background. And you are trusting one vendor's vault and approval flow with the keys to a lot of doors — convenient, and a concentration risk you should choose with your eyes open.

5. Policy and audit engines — IDENTOS PolicyArc

How it works: Instead of managing credentials agent by agent, you define policy in one place: who and what can access which resources, for which tasks, for how long — and you get an audit trail across all of it. IDENTOS PolicyArc, which reached general availability on October 23, 2026, is positioned exactly there. As IDENTOS describes it — a vendor claim from its launch materials — PolicyArc is one place to define, enforce, and audit access policy for people and agents, with task-specific, time-limited access grants.

Strength: This is the enterprise-grade answer to the real question, which is not "how does this one agent log in?" but "what is every agent in this organization allowed to reach, and can we prove it later?" Central policy, time limits, and audit in one system is what compliance and security teams will ask for.

Weakness: Weight. A policy engine is infrastructure to evaluate, buy, integrate, and operate. For a solo developer or a three-person team, it can be more machine than the problem needs today. It also only governs the systems you connect to it — an agent with your password typed into a prompt is outside the policy no matter how good the engine is.

Our ranking, plainly: shared passwords are last, and it is not close. Long-lived keys are a distant fourth. Scoped, short-lived tokens are the baseline every developer should aim for today. Per-agent keys with human approval rank first for individual developers and small teams right now, because they fix the worst failure — password exposure — without a platform rebuild. Policy and audit engines rank first for organizations managing many agents across many people, where the audit trail is the point. Pick based on your scale, but do not pick option one.

What to do this week

You do not need to buy anything to start. You need an inventory and the willingness to delete some credentials. Work through this in order — and if you want a structured pass, run our Agent Access Readiness checklist on Pick a Tools alongside it, then read the broader background in our AI Agent Identity hub.

  • Inventory every agent and what it can reach. List every agent, assistant, script, and automation that signs in to anything on your behalf. For each one: what service, what credential, what permissions, who else has that credential. You cannot fix what you have not listed. Most developers find at least one agent they forgot was still running.
  • Kill shared credentials first. Anywhere an agent uses your personal password, stop — this week, not this quarter. Rotate that password, and do not hand the new one to the agent. If the agent breaks, that breakage is information: it tells you the workflow had no safe sign-in path, which is the thing to fix.
  • Scope to least privilege. For every remaining key or token, cut permissions to what the task actually needs. Read-only where read-only works. One project, not the whole account. If a platform only offers an all-or-nothing key, note it as a risk and shorten its life.
  • Make grants time-limited. Prefer short-lived tokens where they exist. Where they do not, put a calendar date on every long-lived key and rotate on schedule. Task-specific, time-limited grants — the model PolicyArc describes — are the target even if you implement them manually for now.
  • Keep audit logs you actually read. A log nobody opens is decoration. Once a week, scan sign-ins and agent actions for the services that matter: anything you do not recognize gets investigated the same day. Separate agent identities make this possible; shared passwords make it pointless.
  • Make revocation one click, and test it. For each agent, know exactly how you would cut its access in under five minutes — and actually test the revoke path once, before you need it during an incident. If revoking one agent means changing your own password and logging yourself out of everything, you still have a shared-credential problem.

When the inventory is done, score yourself honestly with the Agent Access Readiness tool and fix the lowest-scoring area first. The goal for this week is not perfection. It is making sure no agent anywhere is signing in with your personal password.

The honest limits

Some restraint is warranted, because this category is three days old in its current shape and the marketing is running ahead of the standards.

The standards are unsettled. There is no single, widely adopted protocol for agent identity yet. What 1Password ships, what IDENTOS ships, and what the browser-agent platforms build may converge — or may leave you migrating between incompatible approaches in a year. Early adoption buys you safety now at the price of some rework later. For the password-sharing problem, that trade is still worth it. For a full platform commitment, go in knowing it.

Platform lock-in is a real risk. If one vault holds every agent key and one vendor's approval flow gates every sign-in, leaving that vendor becomes a project, not a settings change. That may be an acceptable trade — password managers already hold that position in most of our lives — but count it as a cost, not a footnote.

Small teams may not need an enterprise policy engine yet. If you are two developers with four agents, a written inventory, scoped tokens, and a calendar reminder to rotate keys will carry you further than a policy platform you have not finished integrating. Buy the layer that matches the number of agents and people you actually have. PolicyArc-class tooling earns its keep when "who approved this agent's access, and when does it expire?" becomes a question you cannot answer from memory.

And this is a developer story first, a consumer story later. The Developer Pulse numbers describe developers because developers are the ones wiring agents into real systems today. Consumers handing agents their banking passwords are the next wave of the same problem — which is precisely why the Chase warning matters. The tooling will follow the developers down-market. Your job is to not still be sharing passwords when it arrives.

The bottom line has not changed since the first paragraph. Agents are useful, agents are not going away, and agents need to sign in to things. All of that can be true while "sign in as me, with my password, forever" is a bad answer. This week gave developers the first mainstream alternatives. Use them — starting with the unglamorous work of listing what your agents can reach, and taking your own password back.

FAQ

How do AI agents log in today?
Most agents today log in with credentials borrowed from a person: a shared password, a long-lived API key pasted into a prompt or .env file, or a broad OAuth token. Newer approaches give each agent its own scoped, short-lived credential, or a per-agent key that requires human approval for every sign-in.

What is 1Password for Agents?
1Password for Agents, launched October 22, 2026, is a feature where each AI agent signs in with its own unique digital key instead of your password. You approve every sign-in attempt on your own device, and the actual password never reaches the agent. 1Password lists it as included in its Individual and Family plans.

Why are banks flagging agent activity?
According to Axios reporting, US banks are detecting unverified agentic activity on accounts. An agent signing in with your password from an unfamiliar location or automation pattern is mechanically indistinguishable from account takeover fraud, which is why Chase has warned customers not to share credentials with third-party agents.

What is an agent identity?
An agent identity is a distinct, revocable identity for a single AI agent — separate from any human user — with its own credential, limited permissions, and an audit trail. It lets you grant task-specific, time-limited access and revoke that one agent without changing your own password or breaking other tools.

What should a developer do first?
Inventory every agent you run and what it can reach, then kill shared credentials first. Move agents to scoped, short-lived, or per-agent credentials, add time limits and audit logs, and make sure you can revoke any single agent in one click.

What is IDENTOS PolicyArc?
IDENTOS PolicyArc, which reached general availability on October 23, 2026, is described by IDENTOS as a single place to define, enforce, and audit access policy for people and agents, including task-specific, time-limited access grants.

Weakness: Everything else. The credential has your full permissions — no scoping, no expiry, no way to tell agent actions from your actions in a log. If the prompt leaks, the password leaks. If the agent is compromised, you are compromised. Rotating the password breaks every agent using it, so nobody rotates it. If you are doing this today, you are not alone — but you should treat it as an incident waiting for a date, not a workflow.

2. Long-lived API keys — better than a password, worse than you think

How it works: Instead of your password, the agent carries an API key — often created under your account, often with broad permissions, often valid until someone remembers to delete it.

Strength: At least it is separate from your human login, and most platforms let you revoke a key without changing your password. For machine-to-machine calls to a single API, this is a reasonable baseline.

Weakness: "Long-lived" is the problem. Keys get copied into repos, CI logs, screenshots, and chat transcripts. They rarely expire, rarely get scoped tightly, and rarely have a human in the loop when they are used. A leaked long-lived key with broad scope is a password with better branding.

3. Scoped, short-lived tokens — the right shape

How it works: The agent gets an OAuth-style token limited to specific permissions, for a specific service, for a short window — minutes or hours, not months. When the window closes, the token dies and a new one must be issued.

Strength: This is the pattern security teams actually want. Least privilege by default, automatic expiry, and a much smaller blast radius if a token leaks. A stolen token that expires in an hour and can only read one project is a bad day. A stolen password is a bad quarter.

Weakness: Support is uneven. Plenty of tools your agents need still do not offer fine-grained, short-lived tokens, and wiring up issuance and refresh for every agent and every service is real engineering work. The pattern is right; the ecosystem is still catching up.

4. Per-agent keys with human approval — 1Password for Agents

How it works: Each agent gets its own identity instead of borrowing yours. 1Password for Agents, launched October 22, 2026, is the clearest consumer-and-developer example so far. As 1Password describes it — a vendor claim, based on its launch materials — each AI agent signs in with its own unique digital key, you approve every sign-in attempt on your own device, and the actual password never reaches the agent. 1Password lists the feature as included in its Individual and Family plans via 1Password.com.

1Password names its launch partners as rolling out, including Meta's Muse and Grok Bot, with Claude Duet, ChatGPT Work/dots, and Townie listed as coming soon. It also says integrations are being built by Browserbase, Browser Use, Perplexity, and Ramp. Treat that partner list as a vendor roadmap claim until each integration is live and documented — but note the shape of it: browser agents and finance tooling are exactly where credential-sharing risk is highest.

Strength: The password never reaches the agent, every sign-in needs your approval on your device, and each agent is distinguishable from you and from every other agent. Revoking one agent does not mean changing your password everywhere.

Weakness: Human approval does not scale forever. Approving every sign-in works for high-value logins; it will chafe for agents that authenticate constantly in the background. And you are trusting one vendor's vault and approval flow with the keys to a lot of doors — convenient, and a concentration risk you should choose with your eyes open.

5. Policy and audit engines — IDENTOS PolicyArc

How it works: Instead of managing credentials agent by agent, you define policy in one place: who and what can access which resources, for which tasks, for how long — and you get an audit trail across all of it. IDENTOS PolicyArc, which reached general availability on October 23, 2026, is positioned exactly there. As IDENTOS describes it — a vendor claim from its launch materials — PolicyArc is one place to define, enforce, and audit access policy for people and agents, with task-specific, time-limited access grants.

Strength: This is the enterprise-grade answer to the real question, which is not "how does this one agent log in?" but "what is every agent in this organization allowed to reach, and can we prove it later?" Central policy, time limits, and audit in one system is what compliance and security teams will ask for.

Weakness: Weight. A policy engine is infrastructure to evaluate, buy, integrate, and operate. For a solo developer or a three-person team, it can be more machine than the problem needs today. It also only governs the systems you connect to it — an agent with your password typed into a prompt is outside the policy no matter how good the engine is.

Our ranking, plainly: shared passwords are last, and it is not close. Long-lived keys are a distant fourth. Scoped, short-lived tokens are the baseline every developer should aim for today. Per-agent keys with human approval rank first for individual developers and small teams right now, because they fix the worst failure — password exposure — without a platform rebuild. Policy and audit engines rank first for organizations managing many agents across many people, where the audit trail is the point. Pick based on your scale, but do not pick option one.

What to do this week

You do not need to buy anything to start. You need an inventory and the willingness to delete some credentials. Work through this in order — and if you want a structured pass, run our Agent Access Readiness checklist on Pick a Tools alongside it, then read the broader background in our AI Agent Identity hub.

  • Inventory every agent and what it can reach. List every agent, assistant, script, and automation that signs in to anything on your behalf. For each one: what service, what credential, what permissions, who else has that credential. You cannot fix what you have not listed. Most developers find at least one agent they forgot was still running.
  • Kill shared credentials first. Anywhere an agent uses your personal password, stop — this week, not this quarter. Rotate that password, and do not hand the new one to the agent. If the agent breaks, that breakage is information: it tells you the workflow had no safe sign-in path, which is the thing to fix.
  • Scope to least privilege. For every remaining key or token, cut permissions to what the task actually needs. Read-only where read-only works. One project, not the whole account. If a platform only offers an all-or-nothing key, note it as a risk and shorten its life.
  • Make grants time-limited. Prefer short-lived tokens where they exist. Where they do not, put a calendar date on every long-lived key and rotate on schedule. Task-specific, time-limited grants — the model PolicyArc describes — are the target even if you implement them manually for now.
  • Keep audit logs you actually read. A log nobody opens is decoration. Once a week, scan sign-ins and agent actions for the services that matter: anything you do not recognize gets investigated the same day. Separate agent identities make this possible; shared passwords make it pointless.
  • Make revocation one click, and test it. For each agent, know exactly how you would cut its access in under five minutes — and actually test the revoke path once, before you need it during an incident. If revoking one agent means changing your own password and logging yourself out of everything, you still have a shared-credential problem.

When the inventory is done, score yourself honestly with the Agent Access Readiness tool and fix the lowest-scoring area first. The goal for this week is not perfection. It is making sure no agent anywhere is signing in with your personal password.

The honest limits

Some restraint is warranted, because this category is three days old in its current shape and the marketing is running ahead of the standards.

The standards are unsettled. There is no single, widely adopted protocol for agent identity yet. What 1Password ships, what IDENTOS ships, and what the browser-agent platforms build may converge — or may leave you migrating between incompatible approaches in a year. Early adoption buys you safety now at the price of some rework later. For the password-sharing problem, that trade is still worth it. For a full platform commitment, go in knowing it.

Platform lock-in is a real risk. If one vault holds every agent key and one vendor's approval flow gates every sign-in, leaving that vendor becomes a project, not a settings change. That may be an acceptable trade — password managers already hold that position in most of our lives — but count it as a cost, not a footnote.

Small teams may not need an enterprise policy engine yet. If you are two developers with four agents, a written inventory, scoped tokens, and a calendar reminder to rotate keys will carry you further than a policy platform you have not finished integrating. Buy the layer that matches the number of agents and people you actually have. PolicyArc-class tooling earns its keep when "who approved this agent's access, and when does it expire?" becomes a question you cannot answer from memory.

And this is a developer story first, a consumer story later. The Developer Pulse numbers describe developers because developers are the ones wiring agents into real systems today. Consumers handing agents their banking passwords are the next wave of the same problem — which is precisely why the Chase warning matters. The tooling will follow the developers down-market. Your job is to not still be sharing passwords when it arrives.

The bottom line has not changed since the first paragraph. Agents are useful, agents are not going away, and agents need to sign in to things. All of that can be true while "sign in as me, with my password, forever" is a bad answer. This week gave developers the first mainstream alternatives. Use them — starting with the unglamorous work of listing what your agents can reach, and taking your own password back.

FAQ

How do AI agents log in today?
Most agents today log in with credentials borrowed from a person: a shared password, a long-lived API key pasted into a prompt or .env file, or a broad OAuth token. Newer approaches give each agent its own scoped, short-lived credential, or a per-agent key that requires human approval for every sign-in.

According to Axios reporting, US banks are detecting unverified agentic activity on accounts. An agent signing in with your password from an unfamiliar location or automation pattern is mechanically indistinguishable from account takeover fraud, which is why Chase has warned customers not to share credentials with third-party agents.

What is an agent identity?
An agent identity is a distinct, revocable identity for a single AI agent — separate from any human user — with its own credential, limited permissions, and an audit trail. It lets you grant task-specific, time-limited access and revoke that one agent without changing your own password or breaking other tools.

What should a developer do first?
Inventory every agent you run and what it can reach, then kill shared credentials first. Move agents to scoped, short-lived, or per-agent credentials, add time limits and audit logs, and make sure you can revoke any single agent in one click.

title: A Passkey Deployment Checklist Beyond the Happy-Path Demo
summary:
Creating a passkey once on your laptop is not the same as deploying passkeys.

A production release needs evidence at three layers: public configuration, server verification, and the real user journey. A failure at any layer can produce a broken experience even when the other two look healthy.

This is part two of Passkeys in Production, adapted from our full deployment checklist. Helpers.work also provides the Passkey Deployment Checker used for the public-configuration layer.

1. Record the identity boundary

Write down the actual sign-in origin, RP ID, allowed server origins, credential store, and native app identifiers.

An illustrative setup:

Sign-in origin: https://login.example.com
RP ID:          example.com
Server policy:  explicitly allow https://login.example.com

The RP ID is not necessarily the hostname visible in the address bar. Read it from the options your backend produces.

Keep staging and production boundaries intentional. A parent-domain RP ID combined with overly broad server origin acceptance can expose production authentication to weaker environments.

2. Check public HTTPS

Verify the real login hostname, not only the marketing site:

  • DNS resolves to the intended service.
  • The certificate covers that hostname.
  • The server sends a complete chain.
  • HTTPS redirects stay on HTTPS.
  • Renewal and expiry monitoring are working.

The SSL Certificate Checker can help identify certificate problems. A valid certificate on the apex domain is not proof that every login subdomain is configured correctly.

Localhost development exceptions do not make HTTP production suitable. A public checker also should not be used to scan private infrastructure.

3. Publish only the files you need

Deployment feature Relevant configuration
Ordinary single-domain web sign-in HTTPS, eligible RP ID, server verification
Cross-domain use of one RP ID /.well-known/webauthn
Credential-manager discovery Optional /.well-known/passkey-endpoints
Native Apple app Associated Domains and webcredentials
Native Android app Digital Asset Links and release signing identity

Sibling subdomains using an eligible common parent RP ID do not normally need Related Origin Requests. They still need explicit server origin validation.

4. Inspect the deployed response

A reverse proxy can turn a well-known request into a redirect or an HTML application shell. Inspect status, headers, and body together:

curl --proto '=https' --max-time 15 --silent --show-error --include \
  https://example.com/.well-known/passkey-endpoints

Replace the example domain with your RP ID. This command leaves redirects visible instead of following them.

An illustrative discovery document:

{
  "enroll": "https://example.com/account/passkeys/new",
  "manage": "https://example.com/account/passkeys"
}

The JSON should be publicly retrievable. The account pages themselves can require authentication and must enforce your enrollment policy.

These are user-facing discovery links, not WebAuthn verification APIs. An absent passkey-endpoints document does not by itself break sign-in.

5. Verify mobile release identity

For Apple, the public association file and the app's entitlement must agree. Check webcredentials, not just applinks, and preserve existing association sections.

For Android, compare the package name and signing-certificate fingerprint for the build users actually install. A debug certificate or upload certificate can differ from the distribution certificate.

The credential-sharing relation is delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds. Follow the Android prerequisites for the surrounding configuration.

A public file scanner cannot inspect your installed binary or force platform association caches to refresh. Test the distributed app.

6. Exercise the backend rejection paths

Use a maintained verifier, then test your own wiring:

  • Unexpected, expired, and replayed challenges are rejected.
  • Unapproved origins are rejected.
  • The RP ID context must match.
  • Required presence and verification flags are enforced.
  • A credential cannot authenticate a different account.
  • Revoked credentials cannot start a new session.

Challenges should be bound to the intended operation and consumed reliably. Do not allow concurrent requests to make a completed challenge reusable.

Be careful with signature counters. Some authenticators and synced credentials do not supply a useful monotonic counter. Apply the library's documented policy rather than treating every non-increase as definitive evidence of cloning.

7. Test the lifecycle

First enrollment is only the start. Test sign-out, sign-in, prompt cancellation, second-credential enrollment, revocation, device loss, and recovery.

Include the browsers, operating systems, credential providers, and mobile builds your audience actually uses. Conditional UI and related-origin support can differ from basic WebAuthn support.

Keep fallback explicit. An unsupported client should not trigger a hidden bypass of origin or verification policy.

8. Plan rollback without locking users out

Stopping new enrollments and stopping existing passkey authentication are different changes. During an incident, the second can strand users who no longer have another sign-in method.

Preserve credential records and the RP ID through an ordinary frontend rollback. Test recovery before removing passwords, and decide which recovered sessions may immediately enroll a new credential.

Track aggregate completion and failure categories without collecting raw credential payloads as routine analytics.

The release gate

Run the Passkey Deployment Checker with your actual RP ID and expected app values. Then complete server and real-device tests.

No public scan can prove your challenge storage, account mapping, session issuance, or recovery process is correct.

Continue with RP ID and related origins, or use the report interpretation guide. New to the model? Start with passkeys explained.

References: W3C WebAuthn, passkey endpoints, and Apple associated domains.

title: How to Read a Passkey Deployment Checker Report
summary:
A website can have valid passkey metadata and a broken authentication flow. It can also support passkeys while publishing none of the optional discovery files a scanner looks for.

The useful question is not "How many green checks do I have?" It is "Which conditions did this report evaluate, and which of them does my architecture require?"

This is the final part of Passkeys in Production, adapted from the full report guide. We build the Helpers.work Passkey Deployment Checker; this walkthrough describes its actual scope.

Use the origin where WebAuthn runs

Enter your public sign-in URL or domain. The tool normalizes it to an origin, so supplying /account/security does not turn the scan into a test of that page.

If the marketing site redirects to a login host, use the host where the browser actually creates or requests credentials.

The checker uses public HTTPS domains on port 443. It does not scan localhost, IP-literal targets, private networks, custom website ports, or URLs containing embedded credentials.

Those are tool restrictions. They are not a claim that every excluded environment is inherently unsupported by WebAuthn.

Enter your real RP ID

The most important advanced field is the RP ID.

Website: https://login.example.com
RP ID:   example.com

This illustrative setup may be intentional. If you omit the RP ID, the tool instead uses login.example.com and marks the source as inferred.

That is a default, not reliable discovery. Read publicKey.rp.id in registration options and publicKey.rpId in authentication options from your backend.

See the RP ID guide if the domain relationship is unclear.

Know the six checks

Check What it evaluates
HTTPS Configuration Public connectivity and normal certificate validation
RP ID Compatibility Website-to-RP relationship for the supplied inputs
Related Origins RP-host /.well-known/webauthn and applicable origins
Passkey Endpoints Optional discovery metadata and URL syntax
Apple App Site Association Public webcredentials declarations
Android Asset Links Public credential-sharing statements and expected identity

HTTPS and RP ID checks are always evaluated. Related origins and passkey endpoints are selected by default; mobile checks are opt-in.

An unrelated RP ID forces the required related-origin evaluation even if the optional selection is off.

For native apps, provide expected identifiers and the actual release signing-certificate fingerprint when available. Without expected values, valid JSON for another app is not proof that your app is configured.

Read statuses instead of inventing a score

Status Meaning
passed The evaluated condition passed for these inputs
warning A concern or compatibility limitation needs review
failed The evaluated condition failed
not_applicable Not selected, or optional configuration is not applicable
unknown The checker could not reach a reliable conclusion

The report-level success value means a report was produced. It does not mean all checks passed.

A required related-origin failure can block your intended cross-domain flow. A missing optional discovery document may not affect sign-in at all. A network timeout should not be relabeled as either a pass or a confirmed deployment defect.

Three examples of useful interpretation

These are hypothetical scenarios, not live scan results.

The web-only application

The site uses an eligible RP ID and has no native apps. Apple and Android association files are not relevant to that deployment.

A missing /.well-known/passkey-endpoints file is also not proof that passkeys are unavailable. It is optional metadata for helping clients find enrollment and management pages.

Focus on the actual registration and authentication ceremony.

The cross-domain application

The browser runs at https://example.co.uk and requests RP ID example.com.

Inspect https://example.com/.well-known/webauthn. Verify the calling origin is represented, the body is usable JSON, and the client supports the mechanism.

The backend still needs explicit origin acceptance and the correct credential records.

The Android release-only failure

The public file may contain a debug or upload-certificate fingerprint rather than the certificate on the distributed app.

Compare package name, credential-sharing relation, and release signing identity together. The scanner cannot inspect the installed binary or app manifest.

Some green results have important limits

A passkey-endpoints result validates advertised URLs syntactically. It does not visit those URLs or exercise enrollment.

An Apple association result does not verify the app entitlement or Apple's cached state. An Android result does not verify the manifest, resources, or installed signing certificate.

An HTTPS result is not a full TLS audit. It does not evaluate every cipher, security header, or route.

And no public configuration report verifies challenge freshness, assertion signatures, account mapping, session issuance, or account recovery.

Fix the failed layer, then test again

Work from DNS and HTTPS toward RP ID, required files, clients, and the server ceremony.

An HTML response with status 200 often points to a catch-all route, not malformed JSON. Redirect handling also differs: this checker follows bounded HTTPS redirects for related origins but treats passkey-endpoint and app-association redirects differently.

After deployment, inspect the public response rather than assuming the local file is already visible through the CDN.

Then register, sign out, sign in, cancel, revoke, and recover on your supported clients. Use the production checklist as the final release gate.

For the conceptual foundation, see passkeys explained. Technical references: W3C passkey endpoints, Apple associated domains, and Android prerequisites.

title: Docker Reported Exit 0. The Kernel Had Already OOM-Killed It.
summary:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates.

The notification I expected to be a config mistake

My NAS sent the notification every Docker user learns to skim: container
stopped unexpectedly. This one is the edge proxy in front of my

403 responses            33,636   (geoblock / deny-list doing its job)
429 responses            16,082   (inflight and rate limiting doing their job)

host load average        26–32

knocking: this container is the public edge for a multi-terabyte Wikipedia

cloud, and the responses telling it to go away are still work.

     limits:
-      memory: 512M
+      memory: 2g

+memswap_limit: 2g

order-of-magnitude bigger flood reaches 2 GB too. The real fix is shrinking
the public entry surface, not enlarging the cage around it — and a limit
bump that is not labelled as a stopgap becomes a permanent explanation.

already had 16 GB of its 40 GB swap in use with committed memory at 92 GB,

title: The 3 Ways DevOps Transformations Actually Fail (And the Fourth Team That Avoided All Three)
summary:
TL;DR: DevOps transformations don't usually fail from lack of budget or lack of tools. They fail from one of three predictable anti-patterns: hiring a single "DevOps engineer" and expecting them to fix everything, buying tooling before fixing the underlying workflow, or trying to automate every step at once. A Lahore e-commerce team's six-month rebuild (deploys: once per 3 weeks → daily; lead time: 6 days → 2 hours; change-failure rate: 22% → 4%) worked specifically because it avoided all three.

Most writing about DevOps leads with what it is or what it measures. Worth flipping that: the more useful question for a team starting (or re-starting) a transformation is what actually kills the attempt, because the failure modes are far more predictable than the success stories suggest.

Anti-pattern 1: "We hired a DevOps engineer, we're covered"

This is the most common first move, and it's structurally wrong. DevOps isn't a job title, it's the removal of the wall between the people who write code and the people who run it, plus automating the manual build-test-deploy grind. Hiring one person to "do DevOps" recreates the wall with a staff of one: that person becomes the new bottleneck, the new single point of failure, and everyone else keeps treating delivery as someone else's problem.

What to do instead: treat DevOps as a practice the existing engineering team adopts, not a role bolted onto the org chart. If you're going to hire, hire someone to build the paved road, not to personally walk every deploy down it.

Anti-pattern 2: buying tools before fixing the workflow

A CI/CD platform, an IaC tool, and an observability stack don't fix a broken release process, they just make the broken process run faster. If your actual problem is that nobody agrees on what "ready to deploy" means, or testing happens inconsistently, a new tool automates that inconsistency instead of removing it.

What to do instead: map the current release process first, find where it actually breaks down (missing tests, manual approval bottlenecks, no rollback plan), fix that step, then pick tooling that supports the fixed process. Tools should follow the workflow decision, not substitute for it.

Anti-pattern 3: automating everything at once

Big-bang rollouts lose support fast, because they ask every team to change every habit simultaneously, with no early win to build confidence. Teams revert to the old process the first time the new one has a rough week, and the whole investment stalls.

What to do instead: automate the single most painful step first (often manual deployment or manual testing), ship that win, then expand. Momentum from one early success carries the rest of the rollout further than a comprehensive plan announced on day one.

The five practices and four metrics, for reference

Once the three anti-patterns are avoided, these are what you're actually building and measuring:

Practice What it does
CI/CD Automates build, test, and ship on every code change
Infrastructure as Code Version-controls servers/networks, prevents drift
Automated testing Catches broken changes before customers do
Observability Reveals production behavior via logs, metrics, traces
Shared-ownership culture The team that writes the code also runs it
DORA metric Elite Low
Deployment frequency On-demand, many/day Weekly–monthly
Lead time for changes <1 hour 1 week–1 month
Change failure rate ~5% or lower Often >30%
Time to restore service <1 hour Days

Case study: the team that didn't make any of the three mistakes

A Lahore e-commerce team started at once-per-three-weeks deploys, 6-day lead time, 22% change-failure rate, and manual evening releases that regularly broke production. What they didn't do matters as much as what they did:

  • They didn't hire a single DevOps engineer and hand them the problem, developers paired with the build team throughout, so the whole team owned the result.
  • They didn't buy a tool stack first, the GitHub Actions pipeline and Terraform environments got picked after mapping where the existing process actually broke.
  • They didn't automate everything simultaneously, automated testing and staged rollout came before the full observability buildout, sequenced to bank an early win.
Metric Before After 6 months
Deployment frequency 1 per 3 weeks Daily
Lead time 6 days 2 hours
Change-failure rate 22% 4%
Incident hours — −35% per month

Six months, not six weeks, not two years, sequenced specifically to avoid the three failure modes above rather than racing to implement every practice in parallel.

FAQ

Which of the three anti-patterns is the most common one you see?
Hiring a single DevOps engineer and expecting the team's culture to change around them, it's the path of least organizational resistance, which is exactly why it doesn't work, nothing about the team's actual habits changed.

If we've already made one of these mistakes, is it reversible?
Yes. A team that already hired a single DevOps engineer can still shift to shared ownership, it just means that person's job becomes building paved roads for others instead of personally operating the pipeline.

Is six months a realistic timeline for most teams, or was this case study unusually fast?
Six months for a full shift across all five practices is realistic for a team of meaningful size with committed pairing time. Automating the single most painful step (anti-pattern 3's fix) can show results in weeks, the full DORA-metric shift takes longer.

Originally published on the Sherdil Cloud blog, the full piece (with the complete five-practice and four-metric breakdown) is here. For the hands-on pipeline build, see CI/CD pipeline from scratch; for a startup-specific sequencing of this, DevOps best practices for startups.

About the author: Muhammad Usman is Head of DevOps at Sherdil Cloud, AWS DevOps Engineer Professional, Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), and Alibaba Cloud Certified, building cloud and DevOps infrastructure for enterprises across Pakistan, the UAE, and the United States since 2014.

title: Building a Local AI SOC Lab with Wazuh and Qwen: Lessons from a Real Implementation
summary:
Security monitoring generates a lot of data. But collecting alerts is only the beginning. The real challenge is retrieving the right events, understanding what happened, and making decisions based on evidence.

I wanted to explore a practical question:

Can a locally hosted AI model help a security analyst investigate Wazuh alerts without giving the AI control over the infrastructure?

To explore this, I built an isolated AI-assisted Security Operations Center (SOC) lab using Wazuh, OpenSearch, Python, SQLite, and a local Qwen model.

I tested synthetic log content containing text designed to manipulate the model into treating failed authentication as successful authentication.

In a documented retest, the model preserved the failed-login finding.

These were limited experiments.

They do not demonstrate complete resistance to prompt injection or guarantee that every AI-generated recommendation is safe.

Security logs are evidence, not instructions.

Human review remains essential.

I wanted the project to demonstrate more than a working screenshot.

The implementation also includes validation of event identity, persistent processing state, structured model responses, and read-only operational boundaries.

The lab still has important limitations: manual execution, no continuous alert monitoring, and network restrictions around the local model service that require further verification before broader deployment.

First, reliable data retrieval comes before AI analysis. Missing alerts can undermine even a well-written incident report.

Second, local AI can assist security investigations, but its output must be validated. A structured response is not necessarily a correct response.

Third, automation needs clear security boundaries. I prefer a system that helps an analyst understand an event over one that performs potentially harmful actions without approval.

title: php -v over SSH doesn’t tell you which PHP your website runs
summary:
After a PHP release, the quickest check is to SSH in and type php -v. I've done that myself. For this post I set up a test machine to see how much that number says about the website. Not much.

php -v reports the command-line PHP. Your site is served by whatever PHP the web server hands requests to, and on the same box those can be different builds, different versions, with different extensions and different php.ini files.

Same machine, two answers

I put this together on Ubuntu 24.04: Apache 2.4.58 passing .php requests to PHP-FPM 8.3, and the php command pointing at the PHP 8.4 CLI that was already installed. Then I asked each side who it was.

How I checked Result
php -v over SSH PHP 8.4.21 (cli)
PHP_VERSION from a page in the browser 8.3.6
PHP_SAPI on the command line cli
PHP_SAPI in the browser fpm-fcgi
php.ini loaded on the command line /etc/php/8.4/cli/php.ini
php.ini loaded in the browser /etc/php/8.3/fpm/php.ini
WordPress Site Health, opened in the browser 8.3.6, fpm-fcgi
The same Site Health data, read from the CLI 8.4.21, cli

None of this is new. The PHP manual's chapter on the command line covers the separate SAPI and the separate php.ini. Seeing the two side by side on one machine shows how easy it is to check the wrong one and call it done.

Why they drift apart

On Ubuntu, each PHP version and each SAPI is its own package: php8.3-cli, php8.3-fpm, php8.4-cli, and so on. The bare php command is a symlink to one of them.

$ which -a php php8.3 php8.4
/usr/bin/php
/usr/bin/php8.3
/usr/bin/php8.4
$ ls -l /usr/bin/php
/usr/bin/php -> /etc/alternatives/php

Here it pointed at 8.4. The web server config sent requests to php-fpm8.3. Those two choices are made in different places, by different people sometimes, and nothing keeps them in sync.

It wasn't only the version

Halfway through, WordPress refused to load in the browser:

Your PHP installation appears to be missing the MySQL extension which is required by WordPress.
Please check that the mysqli PHP extension is installed and enabled.

From the command line, the same WordPress install worked fine. The 8.4 CLI had mysqli. The 8.3 FPM didn't. php -m happily listed mysqli, because php -m was asking the CLI. Installing php8.3-mysql and restarting FPM fixed the browser side.

So the gap covers extensions and ini settings as well as the version number. A check run from the CLI only tells you about the CLI.

Checking the PHP your site actually runs

The answer has to come from a web request.

A tiny file does it. Give it a name nobody will guess, open it in the browser, then delete it:


header('Content-Type: text/plain');
printf("PHP_VERSION=%s\nPHP_SAPI=%s\nphp.ini=%s\n",
    PHP_VERSION, PHP_SAPI, php_ini_loaded_file());

PHP_VERSION=8.3.6
PHP_SAPI=fpm-fcgi
php.ini=/etc/php/8.3/fpm/php.ini

phpinfo() tells you the same and much more. I prefer the small file, because forgetting to delete it costs less.

On WordPress you don't need a file at all. Tools → Site Health → Info → Server shows the PHP version and SAPI, and since you open it in the browser, it's the web PHP.

The catch: WP-CLI runs on the CLI PHP. When I pulled the same Site Health data from the command line, it reported 8.4.21 and cli. If you check from WP-CLI, you're checking the wrong PHP again, just more politely.

== Web
php_version: 8.3.6 (Supports 64bit values)
php_sapi: fpm-fcgi
== CLI
php_version: 8.4.21 (Supports 64bit values)
php_sapi: cli

What I check now

When I want to know whether a PHP update reached my site, I check from the browser side: the small file, phpinfo(), or Site Health. php -v and WP-CLI tell me about the shell. That's still useful, for cron jobs and CLI scripts, but it isn't the answer to "is my website patched?"

One thing I didn't test: what happens when the FPM package updates but the FPM service hasn't restarted yet. I'd expect the old binary to keep serving until a restart, but I haven't measured it, so I won't claim it.

What does php -v say on your server, and does it match what your website reports?

I build WordPress plugins and write about them at https://raplsworks.com/.

Disclaimer: The tests were run on a test machine I set up for this post. English isn't my first language, so I use an AI assistant to help draft and edit the writing.
